title: Secondary sex ratio among women exposed to diethylstilbestrol in utero.
ehr_evidence: Data were provided by women participating in the National Cancer Institute (NCI) DES Combined Cohort Study, with information collected via mailed questionnaires (1994 and 1997) and telephone interviews; DES exposure status was verified by medical record.
summary: In a US combined cohort of parous women exposed to DES in utero and unexposed women, in utero DES exposure was not associated with secondary sex ratio overall, but higher odds of male births were observed among women first exposed earlier in gestation to higher cumulative doses.
key_findings: No overall association between in utero DES exposure and secondary sex ratio: adjusted OR 1.05 (95% CI, 0.95–1.17) for having a male birth comparing DES-exposed to unexposed women.
Odds of conceiving a male birth increased with increasing DES dose (p-trend = 0.038).
Among women with complete data on dose and timing (33%), first exposure at < 13 weeks to ≥ 5 g DES had the highest odds of a male birth (adjusted OR 1.24, 95% CI, 1.04–1.48) versus no exposure.
No statistically significant trend by gestational age at first DES exposure (p-trend = 0.186).
Among first births only, the fully adjusted OR for having a male birth was 1.37 (95% CI, 1.06–1.77) for first exposure at < 13 weeks to ≥ 5 g versus no exposure.
captured_features: DES exposure status (verified by medical record)
cumulative DES dose (< 5 g vs ≥ 5 g)
gestational age at first DES exposure (< 13 vs ≥ 13 weeks)
offspring sex / proportion of male births (secondary sex ratio)
pathologies_diseases: None (outcome is secondary sex ratio, a reproductive measure, not a disease)
study_design: Cohort (combined prospective/retrospective cohort of DES-exposed and unexposed women)
data_source_type: other (research cohort using mailed questionnaires and telephone interviews)
population: US parous women exposed to DES in utero (DES daughters) and unexposed women from the NCI DES Combined Cohort Study, born in the 1950s–1960s, analyzed in the mid-1990s
limitations: High proportion of missing data on DES dose and timing (67% of exposed women), limiting dose-response analysis.
ORs overestimate prevalence ratios because the outcome (male birth) is common.
Exposure information varied in completeness across cohorts, and dose was imputed from field-center medians for women with missing data.
